prompt: The deploy portal took 1,100 engineer-hours. At Coreto's loaded cost of R$ 150 an hour, what did it cost, in reais?
What did the three services that deploy through the portal have in common?
hint: What did their owners do before the portal?

choices.text: They belonged to the Platform team
choices.why: The autopsy does not say so; what it found was about how they deployed before.

choices.text: Their teams had been in the launch demo, and so had seen how it worked
choices.why: The demo and the guide moved nobody; seeing it was not what made the difference.

choices.text: None had a deploy pipeline before it
choices.why: Right: they had deployed by asking Platform, so the portal was a real gain; the 38 with pipelines gained a step.

choices.text: They were the newest services at Coreto
choices.why: Age was not the pattern; having no pipeline was.

prompt: Somebody argues: "We spent R$ 165,000 on the portal, so teams should be told to use it." What is wrong with the argument?
hint: Can any decision today get the money back?

choices.text: The money is sunk, and no option gets any of it back
choices.why: Right: no option recovers the R$ 165,000, and forcing use would also hide what adoption measures.

choices.text: The figure is wrong; the true cost is higher
choices.why: The figure is right at R$ 150 an hour; the flaw is letting spent money steer the decision at all.

choices.text: The CFO, not engineering, decides what to do with spent money
choices.why: Whoever decides, spent money is out of the comparison; only future cost and benefit are in it.

choices.text: Mandates are too slow
choices.why: A mandate is fast; that is why it is tempting, and why lesson 14 warns it hides the evidence.

prompt: Six months after launch, 3 of Coreto's 41 services deployed through the portal. What share is that, to the nearest whole percent?
After launch, Platform wrote a better guide and ran a second demo, and usage did not move. What does the autopsy conclude from that?

choices.text: The guide was still too technical
choices.why: A clearer guide answers a question nobody had; the teams knew the portal and did not need it.

choices.text: Teams resist change
choices.why: The same teams adopted the template in lesson 14; they stayed away from a step that added work.

choices.text: Promotion was half done, and a third demo would finish it
choices.why: More of what moved nobody twice is the usual reaction the autopsy replaces.

choices.text: The teams knew about it and had no use for it
choices.why: Right: nobody had stayed away for lack of information, so the problem was upstream, in what was built.

prompt: Match each cause the autopsy found to the evidence for it at Coreto.
hint: Who asked, who benefited, what got shown.

pairs.right: A launch demo, while an investigation ending a proposal showed nothing
Requirements taken from requests in Platform's channel
The interruptions it removed were Platform's
A launch date and no decision date

right_distractors: A budget cut halfway through the build

prompt: Every request in Platform's channel was real, yet the requirements built from them were wrong for most teams. Why?
hint: Who never wrote in that channel?

choices.text: The requests were exaggerated by the teams making them
choices.why: The lesson says the requests were real; the flaw is in who was absent.

choices.text: Platform misread the requests
choices.why: The portal answered those requests well; it was built for the wrong population.

choices.text: Requirements should come from managers rather than engineers
choices.why: The lesson asks for the people whose work would change, whatever their title.

choices.text: Teams with pipelines never wrote there
choices.why: Right: the teams that had no problem to report were invisible, so the tool fitted the loud few.

prompt: The lesson gives one short test for whose problem a tool solves. What is it?

choices.text: Who will maintain it?
choices.why: Maintenance matters for future cost, but it does not say who benefits.

choices.text: Whose week gets easier?
choices.why: Right: for the portal the answer was Platform's, which made it an internal efficiency project.

choices.text: How many people asked for it in the channel?
choices.why: Counting requests repeats the portal's mistake: it counts the loud and skips the silent.

choices.text: Does it have a demo for the engineering review?
choices.why: A demo is the visibility that pulled Coreto towards building in the first place.

prompt: By the lesson, a project with no decision date is decided by ___, which always says "nearly done".
hint: What keeps a moving thing moving.

prompt: What did Helena Prates change after reading the autopsy?

choices.text: Every tool now needs her approval before work starts
choices.why: A gate at the top does not change what the teams are rewarded for.

choices.text: The engineers who built the portal were moved to other teams
choices.why: The autopsy is blameless, and the lesson names the cause in how work was chosen.

choices.text: Investigations that end a proposal are presented like launches
choices.why: Right: finding out a tool is unnecessary is work, and counting it removes the pull towards building.

choices.text: Platform stopped building internal tools
choices.why: Platform went on to build the template in lesson 14; the change was in how work is chosen.

prompt: Put the four steps the lesson recommends before building an internal tool in order.
hint: You cannot measure a pain nobody has described to you.
items: Ask the people who would use it
Build the smallest thing that removes it
Write the kill date before it ships
trap: Building first and asking at the launch is the portal's order: the answer arrives after the hours are spent.

prompt: Why does Rafaela write the kill date before the tool ships rather than when usage disappoints?
hint: Who is attached to it before anything is spent?

choices.text: So the team knows exactly how long it has to build
choices.why: A kill date judges use after launch; it is not a deadline for the build.

choices.text: Because the CFO requires a date on every project
choices.why: The lesson gives no such rule; the reason is about when a decision is honest.

choices.text: So the tool is certain to be switched off
choices.why: A kill date does not mean the tool dies; it means the decision is taken on evidence at a chosen time.

choices.text: Nobody is attached to it yet
choices.why: Right: decided in advance, the rule is not bent by hours already spent or pride in the work.

prompt: Comparing what to do with the portal now, which figure does Rafaela leave out of the table?
hint: It is the same whatever she picks.

choices.text: The cost of moving three services onto the template's pipeline
choices.why: That is a future cost of one option, so it belongs in the comparison.

choices.text: The hosting and on-call cost of keeping it
choices.why: Future running costs are exactly what the comparison is about.
Right: it is gone whichever option she chooses, so it cannot tell the options apart.

choices.text: What the three users gain
choices.why: What each option gives the people still using it is half of the table.

prompt: Which of these, found in a proposal for an internal tool, are signs the lesson tells you to test? Choose all that apply.
hint: The portal's own history, as a checklist.

choices.text: The requirements came from requests to the team that will build it
choices.why: Right: ask who would change how they work, and whether they were asked.

choices.text: The pain is described but not counted
choices.why: Right: count the hours it costs today before spending hours to remove it.

choices.text: The proposal names the team that will run it
choices.why: Naming an owner is good practice, not one of the warning signs.

choices.text: There is a launch date and nothing after it
choices.why: Right: ask on what date, and at what level of use, the work stops.

prompt: The portal cost R$ 165,000 and three services use it. What did it cost per service that uses it, in reais?
hint: Divide by the services that chose it.

prompt: Coreto's Data team proposes an internal metrics catalogue. Its requirements list comes from the questions other teams ask in Data's channel. By this lesson, what should Davi ask first?
hint: Whose voices does a channel miss?

choices.text: Which teams never ask there, and why
choices.why: Right: the channel hears only the teams with a problem to report, which is the portal's blind spot.

choices.text: Which technology the catalogue will be built on
choices.why: Technology comes after knowing whether anybody beyond the loud few needs it.

choices.text: Whether Data has time to demo it at the engineering review
choices.why: A demo is the visibility that pulls teams towards building; it answers nothing about need.

choices.text: How many questions arrived in the channel last month
choices.why: Counting helps measure the pain, but counting the channel still skips the teams that never write there.

prompt: A tool's kill date arrives and the teams that asked for it are not using it. Its builders want more time to add features. What does the kill date say?
hint: It was agreed when nobody was attached.

choices.text: Give them the time, since features are what was missing
choices.why: That is momentum talking; the rule was written to stop exactly this conversation.

choices.text: Switch it off, move its users back, write down the lesson
choices.why: Right: the decision was taken in advance, on evidence, and the evidence is in.

choices.text: Mandate it for one quarter to get a fair test
choices.why: A mandated quarter measures obedience, which lesson 14 showed tells you nothing.

choices.text: Ask the CTO to decide, since the date was only ever a guideline
choices.why: A date that bends when it arrives was never a decision; that is why it is written before shipping.

prompt: A proposed tool would take 1,100 hours to build. By the lesson's second step, what has to be true of the pain it removes before it is worth building?

choices.text: Several teams must have mentioned it in the channel
choices.why: Mentions are the portal's evidence; they describe the pain without counting it.

choices.text: It must cost more than 1,100 hours over the tool's life
choices.why: Right: a tool that costs 1,100 hours has to save more than that, and the count says whether the pain is that large.

choices.text: It must be felt by Platform
choices.why: Whose pain it is matters for who benefits, but the second step is about its size.

choices.text: It must be severe enough that a demo would impress the engineering review
choices.why: An impressive demo is the visibility that built the portal; it measures nothing about the pain.

prompt: A tool would mostly make the Platform team's own week easier. By the lesson, how should it be treated?
hint: It is allowed; it just has a different name.

choices.text: Rejected, because platform work has to serve other teams
choices.why: The lesson does not forbid it; it asks that it be sized honestly.

choices.text: As internal efficiency, sized by hours saved
choices.why: Right: sized against Platform's own interruptions, not launched as a product for everybody.

choices.text: Launched to every team with a demo, to spread the benefit
choices.why: That is the portal's path: a builders' tool launched as everyone's product.

choices.text: Mandated, since Platform is its own user
choices.why: Nobody else is being asked to use it, so there is nothing to mandate.
